# Plan: rate limiting for the orders API

One customer's script created 40,000 orders in ten minutes last week and slowed every other customer down. I want to add rate limiting to `src/server.ts` and ship it this week.

What we have:

- 3 instances of `src/server.ts` behind a round-robin load balancer.
- A Redis 7 cluster already used for sessions by another service; we may use it.
- `POST /orders` writes to Postgres and is the expensive call; `GET /orders` is cheap.
- About 20 enterprise customers have scripted integrations that legitimately burst.

Not decided yet:

- What to key the limit on: `x-customer-id`, client IP, or both.
- Algorithm: fixed window, sliding window, or token bucket.
- Where counters live: Redis, or in each instance's memory.
- What happens if the counter store is unreachable: let requests through or reject them.
- How enterprise customers get higher limits, and who owns those numbers.
- What a rejected client sees.
- How to roll it out without breaking the enterprise integrations.

content.name: ask

questions.question: Should the rate limiter key on `x-customer-id` rather than client IP or a combination of both?

options.label: Key on `x-customer-id`
options.tradeoff: Matches existing auth model and stops a single customer from spawning many IPs; misses customers who share an ID or leak it, but those are identity/secret-rotation problems.
options.description: Use the required customer header as the sole rate-limit key for both default and enterprise tiers.

options.label: Key on client IP
options.tradeoff: Easy to spoof or rotate via proxies and punishes customers behind NAT or multi-IP integrations; also ignores the actual identity that created the 40k-order spike.
options.description: Use the request's remote address as the rate-limit key.

options.label: Key on both
options.tradeoff: More granular but harder to reason about, can split a legitimate customer's budget across IPs, and needs a fallback when one key is missing.
options.description: Apply separate or combined limits per customer ID plus IP.

options.label: Let the caller choose
options.tradeoff: Maximum flexibility but adds another configuration surface and lets a misconfigured caller bypass protection.
options.description: Make the key strategy configurable per customer or route.

brief.where: `src/server.ts` already rejects requests without `x-customer-id` and uses it for every order lookup and insert.
brief.what: The rate-limit key determines which requests share a budget and therefore whether one customer can exhaust another's capacity.
brief.how: If you accept the recommendation, we will drop IP-based limiting from this design and treat `x-customer-id` as the canonical identity for both default and enterprise limits.

evidence.note: All requests already require x-customer-id, so it is the natural key.

questions.question: Should we use a token-bucket algorithm for the rate limiter?

options.label: Token bucket
options.tradeoff: Lets enterprise integrations burst while bounding long-term rate; slightly more state than fixed window but Redis can store tokens and last-refill time cheaply.
options.description: Each customer has a bucket that refills at a steady rate and can spend tokens for each request.

options.label: Sliding window
options.tradeoff: Smoothest enforcement but requires keeping per-request timestamps or a rolling Redis sorted set, which is heavier for high throughput.
options.description: Count requests in a rolling time window.

options.label: Fixed window
options.tradeoff: Simplest to implement but creates a thundering-herd problem at window boundaries, exactly when enterprise scripts are likely to burst.
options.description: Count requests in non-overlapping time buckets.

options.label: No algorithm yet; only observe
options.tradeoff: Defers protection and leaves the door open to another 40k-order spike while we gather data.
options.description: Add only request metrics and enforce later.

brief.where: PLAN.md notes 20 enterprise customers have scripted integrations that legitimately burst, while one customer created 40,000 orders in ten minutes.
brief.what: The algorithm decides how bursts are handled and how fair the limit feels to legitimate high-volume customers.
brief.how: If you pick token bucket, we will next settle bucket size, refill rate, and whether those numbers differ by customer tier.

questions.question: Should the rate-limit counters live in the existing Redis 7 cluster rather than in each instance's memory?

options.label: Redis cluster
options.tradeoff: Correct global enforcement across all three instances; adds a network hop and a new failure mode if Redis becomes unreachable.
options.description: Store counters in the existing Redis 7 cluster used by the session service.

options.label: In-memory per instance
options.tradeoff: No extra dependency or latency, but a customer hitting a single instance can use up to 3x the intended budget and limits reset on deploy.
options.description: Keep counters in a local map inside each `src/server.ts` process.

options.label: Hybrid: Redis with in-memory fallback
options.tradeoff: Combines global accuracy with deploy-time resilience, but multiplies the budget when Redis is down and complicates consistency.
options.description: Use Redis normally; fall back to local counters only when Redis is unreachable.

brief.where: PLAN.md says there are 3 load-balanced instances and a Redis 7 cluster already used for sessions by another service.
brief.what: The counter store determines whether enforcement is global or split by instance, and whether rate limiting inherits Redis availability.
brief.how: If you choose Redis, the next round will cover fail-open vs fail-closed behavior when Redis is unreachable; if you choose in-memory, that branch disappears.

questions.question: Should higher limits for enterprise customers be configured per customer by account management or support, with a small set of named tiers?

options.label: Per-customer config owned by account management/support
options.tradeoff: Lets contracts drive the numbers and keeps code out of the critical path; requires a small admin/config workflow for new deals.
options.description: Store enterprise bucket sizes and refill rates in a config table or config file keyed by `x-customer-id`.

options.label: Self-service portal
options.tradeoff: Fastest for scaling but needs a UI, approval workflow, and audit trail; overkill for 20 customers and a one-week ship.
options.description: Let customers or internal teams raise limits through a web form.

options.label: Hardcoded allow-list in code
options.tradeoff: Quickest to ship this week but requires a deploy for every contract change and creates a support bottleneck.
options.description: Maintain a static map of enterprise customer IDs and limits inside `src/server.ts` or a module.

options.label: Same limit for everyone
options.tradeoff: Simplest but likely breaks scripted enterprise integrations and forces a higher default limit that weakens protection.
options.description: Do not offer elevated limits.

brief.where: PLAN.md states about 20 enterprise customers have scripted integrations that legitimately burst.
brief.what: This decides who can raise a customer's limit, where those numbers live, and how quickly they can change.
brief.how: If you accept the recommendation, we will then decide the default tier values, the enterprise multiplier, and whether limits are route-specific.

questions.question: Should rejected requests receive HTTP 429 with a `Retry-After` header and a structured JSON error body?

options.label: 429 with `Retry-After` and JSON body
options.tradeoff: Gives scripts the signal they need to back off but exposes the limit policy; standard and easy for clients to handle.
options.description: Return status 429, include `Retry-After: <seconds>`, and a JSON body with `error`, `limit`, and `retryAfter`.

options.label: 429 with no body
options.tradeoff: Slightly less information leakage but harder for automated clients to understand what happened.
options.description: Return status 429 with no additional payload.

options.label: 503 Service Unavailable
options.tradeoff: Masks rate limiting as an outage, confusing monitoring and client retry logic.
options.description: Return status 503 for throttled requests.

options.label: Drop/close the connection
options.tradeoff: Harshest signal but breaks well-behaved HTTP clients and makes debugging painful.
options.description: Close the TCP connection instead of returning a response.

brief.where: PLAN.md lists `What a rejected client sees` as undecided; `src/server.ts` currently returns plain text errors.
brief.what: The response shape determines whether automated integrations can adapt and how support incidents get triaged.
brief.how: If you choose the recommended option, we will next decide whether to also send rate-limit headers on successful requests and whether GET `/orders` counts toward the same budget.

questions.question: Should the rate limiter key on `x-customer-id` rather than client IP or a combination of both?

options.label: Key on `x-customer-id`
options.tradeoff: Matches existing auth model and stops a single customer from spawning many IPs; misses customers who share an ID or leak it, but those are identity/secret-rotation problems.
options.description: Use the required customer header as the sole rate-limit key for both default and enterprise tiers.

options.label: Key on client IP
options.tradeoff: Easy to spoof or rotate via proxies and punishes customers behind NAT or multi-IP integrations; also ignores the actual identity that created the 40k-order spike.
options.description: Use the request's remote address as the rate-limit key.

options.label: Key on both
options.tradeoff: More granular but harder to reason about, can split a legitimate customer's budget across IPs, and needs a fallback when one key is missing.
options.description: Apply separate or combined limits per customer ID plus IP.

options.label: Let the caller choose
options.tradeoff: Maximum flexibility but adds another configuration surface and lets a misconfigured caller bypass protection.
options.description: Make the key strategy configurable per customer or route.

brief.where: `src/server.ts` already rejects requests without `x-customer-id` and uses it for every order lookup and insert.
brief.what: The rate-limit key determines which requests share a budget and therefore whether one customer can exhaust another's capacity.
brief.how: If you accept the recommendation, we will drop IP-based limiting from this design and treat `x-customer-id` as the canonical identity for both default and enterprise limits.

evidence.note: All requests already require x-customer-id, so it is the natural key.

questions.question: Should we use a token-bucket algorithm for the rate limiter?

options.label: Token bucket
options.tradeoff: Lets enterprise integrations burst while bounding long-term rate; slightly more state than fixed window but Redis can store tokens and last-refill time cheaply.
options.description: Each customer has a bucket that refills at a steady rate and can spend tokens for each request.

options.label: Sliding window
options.tradeoff: Smoothest enforcement but requires keeping per-request timestamps or a rolling Redis sorted set, which is heavier for high throughput.
options.description: Count requests in a rolling time window.

options.label: Fixed window
options.tradeoff: Simplest to implement but creates a thundering-herd problem at window boundaries, exactly when enterprise scripts are likely to burst.
options.description: Count requests in non-overlapping time buckets.

options.label: No algorithm yet; only observe
options.tradeoff: Defers protection and leaves the door open to another 40k-order spike while we gather data.
options.description: Add only request metrics and enforce later.

brief.where: PLAN.md notes 20 enterprise customers have scripted integrations that legitimately burst, while one customer created 40,000 orders in ten minutes.
brief.what: The algorithm decides how bursts are handled and how fair the limit feels to legitimate high-volume customers.
brief.how: If you pick token bucket, we will next settle bucket size, refill rate, and whether those numbers differ by customer tier.

questions.question: Should the rate-limit counters live in the existing Redis 7 cluster rather than in each instance's memory?

options.label: Redis cluster
options.tradeoff: Correct global enforcement across all three instances; adds a network hop and a new failure mode if Redis becomes unreachable.
options.description: Store counters in the existing Redis 7 cluster used by the session service.

options.label: In-memory per instance
options.tradeoff: No extra dependency or latency, but a customer hitting a single instance can use up to 3x the intended budget and limits reset on deploy.
options.description: Keep counters in a local map inside each `src/server.ts` process.

options.label: Hybrid: Redis with in-memory fallback
options.tradeoff: Combines global accuracy with deploy-time resilience, but multiplies the budget when Redis is down and complicates consistency.
options.description: Use Redis normally; fall back to local counters only when Redis is unreachable.

brief.where: PLAN.md says there are 3 load-balanced instances and a Redis 7 cluster already used for sessions by another service.
brief.what: The counter store determines whether enforcement is global or split by instance, and whether rate limiting inherits Redis availability.
brief.how: If you choose Redis, the next round will cover fail-open vs fail-closed behavior when Redis is unreachable; if you choose in-memory, that branch disappears.

questions.question: Should higher limits for enterprise customers be configured per customer by account management or support, with a small set of named tiers?

options.label: Per-customer config owned by account management/support
options.tradeoff: Lets contracts drive the numbers and keeps code out of the critical path; requires a small admin/config workflow for new deals.
options.description: Store enterprise bucket sizes and refill rates in a config table or config file keyed by `x-customer-id`.

options.label: Self-service portal
options.tradeoff: Fastest for scaling but needs a UI, approval workflow, and audit trail; overkill for 20 customers and a one-week ship.
options.description: Let customers or internal teams raise limits through a web form.

options.label: Hardcoded allow-list in code
options.tradeoff: Quickest to ship this week but requires a deploy for every contract change and creates a support bottleneck.
options.description: Maintain a static map of enterprise customer IDs and limits inside `src/server.ts` or a module.

options.label: Same limit for everyone
options.tradeoff: Simplest but likely breaks scripted enterprise integrations and forces a higher default limit that weakens protection.
options.description: Do not offer elevated limits.

brief.where: PLAN.md states about 20 enterprise customers have scripted integrations that legitimately burst.
brief.what: This decides who can raise a customer's limit, where those numbers live, and how quickly they can change.
brief.how: If you accept the recommendation, we will then decide the default tier values, the enterprise multiplier, and whether limits are route-specific.

questions.question: Should rejected requests receive HTTP 429 with a `Retry-After` header and a structured JSON error body?

options.label: 429 with `Retry-After` and JSON body
options.tradeoff: Gives scripts the signal they need to back off but exposes the limit policy; standard and easy for clients to handle.
options.description: Return status 429, include `Retry-After: <seconds>`, and a JSON body with `error`, `limit`, and `retryAfter`.

options.label: 429 with no body
options.tradeoff: Slightly less information leakage but harder for automated clients to understand what happened.
options.description: Return status 429 with no additional payload.

options.label: 503 Service Unavailable
options.tradeoff: Masks rate limiting as an outage, confusing monitoring and client retry logic.
options.description: Return status 503 for throttled requests.

options.label: Drop/close the connection
options.tradeoff: Harshest signal but breaks well-behaved HTTP clients and makes debugging painful.
options.description: Close the TCP connection instead of returning a response.

brief.where: PLAN.md lists `What a rejected client sees` as undecided; `src/server.ts` currently returns plain text errors.
brief.what: The response shape determines whether automated integrations can adapt and how support incidents get triaged.
brief.how: If you choose the recommended option, we will next decide whether to also send rate-limit headers on successful requests and whether GET `/orders` counts toward the same budget.
